report:
**Conclusion: The evidence is mixed and not strong enough to say a clear "yes."**

The most authoritative source—the 2019 Cochrane systematic review (Barnes et al.)—concluded: *"There is insufficient evidence to determine whether hypnotherapy is more effective for smoking cessation than other forms of behavioural support or unassisted quitting. If a benefit is present, current evidence suggests the benefit is small at most."* The review found no clear evidence that hypnotherapy outperforms other approaches.

That said, some evidence is encouraging. An older meta-analysis (Viswesvaran & Schmidt, 1992) identified 48 studies and reported a mean quit rate of ~36% for hypnotherapy. A 2025 systematic review by Ekanayake and Elkins, covering 63 studies from 1968–2022, reported "positive support" for hypnosis in smoking cessation. Individual randomized trials have also suggested hypnotherapy can outperform nicotine replacement therapy in certain settings, and some sources cite quit rates of 20–35% at 12 months.

However, the Cochrane review's cautious conclusion carries the most weight because it assessed randomized controlled trials with long-term follow-up and found methodological limitations across studies. Hypnosis may help some individuals, but the current evidence base does not establish it as clearly superior to other cessation methods.

**Sources:**
- Cochrane review (Barnes et al., 2019): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6568235/
- Cochrane plain-language summary: https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001008_does-hypnotherapy-help-people-who-are-trying-stop-smoking
- NICE rapid review (meta-analysis citation): https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng209/evidence/ph10-rapid-review-of-nonnhs-treatments-for-smoking-cessation-pdf-392073181532
